```{r data-and-score}
w      <- tab("score_weights.csv")
summ   <- tab("score_category_summary.csv")
rob    <- tab("score_robustness.csv")
resn   <- tab("q2_residential_n.csv")
rec    <- tab("coverage_recall_by_category.csv")
recc   <- tab("coverage_recall_corrected.csv")
prop   <- tab("coverage_prop_test.csv")
rl     <- tab("coverage_random_labelling.csv")
logit  <- tab("coverage_logistic.csv")
merr   <- tab("coverage_matcher_error.csv")
score  <- readRDS(file.path(ROOT, "data", "processed", "score_subzone.rds"))

n_res   <- resn$n_residential[resn$cut_off == max(resn$cut_off)]
res_sh  <- resn$share_of_residents[resn$cut_off == max(resn$cut_off)]
n_res2  <- resn$n_residential[resn$cut_off == min(resn$cut_off)]
sc_res  <- score$score[score$residential]
e_rec   <- rec %>% dplyr::filter(grepl("ECDA", set), variant == "strict")
e_cor   <- recc %>% dplyr::filter(set == "ecda")
e_prop  <- prop %>% dplyr::filter(set == "ecda")
e_rl    <- rl %>% dplyr::filter(set == "ecda")
c_rl    <- rl %>% dplyr::filter(set == "chas")
e_or    <- logit %>% dplyr::filter(set == "ecda", term == "maturitynon-mature")
e_fm    <- merr %>% dplyr::filter(set == "ecda", stratum == "accepted match")
e_fmiss <- merr %>% dplyr::filter(set == "ecda", stratum != "accepted match")
r800    <- rob$spearman[rob$column == "score_r800"]
r1200   <- rob$spearman[rob$column == "score_r1200"]
req     <- rob$spearman[rob$column == "score_equal"]
```

# Data and the access score

**Unit and rows.** The unit is the URA Master Plan 2019 subzone [@ura2019mp]. Of the 332 subzones, `r n_res` have at least 1,000 residents in Census 2020 [@singstat2021census], and they hold `r pct(res_sh, 2)` of all residents. These form the residential set used by every analysis (`r n_res2` at a 500-resident cut-off). Airports, reservoirs, ports and industrial estates drop out. All layers use SVY21 (EPSG:3414), so distances are in metres.

**Facilities.** Facility locations come from one OpenStreetMap snapshot (2 November 2026, `r num(sum(summ$osm_features))` scored features) [@osm2026]. Each OSM tag maps to one of six categories through a published lookup table, which also generates the download queries. Hospitals, private facilities and alcohol outlets are not scored.

**Where residents live.** A polygon's centroid can fall in a reservoir or outside an L-shaped subzone. Each subzone's centre is therefore the floor-area-weighted mean of its OSM residential buildings (footprint × storeys). Worker dormitories are excluded, because the census counts only residents. Every residential subzone has such a centre.

**The score.** For each centre we count facilities within 1 km, per category. Counts differ in scale: a median of `r num(summ$median_count[summ$category == "food_services"])` food outlets against `r num(summ$median_count[summ$category == "health"])` clinics. Each count is therefore put on one scale as 100 · log(1 + count) / the maximum over residential subzones. The six category scores are combined with weights equal to each category's share of 2023 household spending [@singstat2024hes] (Table 1). Across residential subzones the composite ranges from `r num(min(sc_res), 0)` to `r num(max(sc_res), 0)`, with a median of `r num(median(sc_res), 1)` (Figure 1).

```{r tab-weights}
knitr::kable(
  w %>% dplyr::transmute(Category = CAT_LAB[category], `Household spending lines (HES 2023)` = hes_lines,
                         `S$ / month` = num(sgd_month, 1), Weight = pct(weight)),
  caption = "Table 1. Category weights from the 2023 Household Expenditure Survey. Retail goods sums two divisions.")
```

```{r fig-score, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Composite access score for the residential subzones.", out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("score_composite_map.png"))
```

The weights carry three caveats. First, spending share is not trip frequency. Second, spending says nothing about variety within a category, so variety is counted separately. Third, the weights are national averages: every subzone is scored on the same basket whatever its residents spend. The score is robust to the weights: equal weights rank subzones almost identically (Spearman `r num(req, 3)`). It is less robust to the radius: 800 m and 1.2 km give `r num(r800, 2)` and `r num(r1200, 2)`, and single subzones move by up to `r num(max(rob$max_rank_shift))` places.

## How complete is OpenStreetMap?

OSM is volunteer-built, so its gaps could bias every later result. We checked one category against a near-complete register: ECDA's licensed preschools [@ecda2026]. Each ECDA centre was matched to an OSM preschool that is both close (≤ 50 m) and similarly named (Jaro-Winkler similarity [@winkler1990]). Matching was one-to-one, using the Hungarian algorithm [@kuhn1955]. We then hand-verified a stratified sample of 160 matched and unmatched pairs.

```{r fig-coverage, fig.cap = "Figure 2. Share of ECDA preschools missing from OSM by subzone, empirical-Bayes shrunk; subzones with fewer than five preschools are grey.", out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("coverage_missrate_map.png"))
```

- **Recall is low.** Only `r pct(e_rec$recall)` of ECDA preschools are in OSM (95% CI `r pct(e_rec$ci_lo)`–`r pct(e_rec$ci_hi)`, Wilson interval [@wilson1927]). The verified sample shows no false matches (`r e_fm$n_incorrect`/`r e_fm$n_checked`) and a `r pct(e_fmiss$rate)` false-miss rate. Correcting for both puts true recall at about `r pct(e_cor$recall_corrected)`. OSM, not the matcher, accounts for most of the gap.
- **Recall is spatially even.** Mature and non-mature towns miss `r pct(e_prop$p_mature)` and `r pct(e_prop$p_nonmature)` of their preschools (two-proportion test, p `r p_fmt(e_prop$p_value)`). The arms could have detected a gap of `r num(e_prop$mdd_pp, 1)` points at 80% power [@cohen1988], so this null result is not just low power.
- **Missed preschools are not clustered.** Random labelling with cross-K [@baddeley2015] finds that missed preschools cluster no more than preschools themselves (p `r p_fmt(e_rl$p_value)`). A logistic model with distance to the CBD gives a non-mature odds ratio of `r num(e_or$OR, 2)`, but that effect rests on a single town, Sengkang.

So OSM counts preschools at a low but roughly even rate. Comparisons between subzones survive, but absolute counts do not: the score is a relative measure. CHAS clinics, reported only as a supplementary benchmark, are less even: missed clinics cluster beyond chance (p `r p_fmt(c_rl$p_value)`). The health category should be read with that in mind. A per-subzone quality flag, built with empirical-Bayes shrinkage [@efron1975], is available to Q2 and Q3 as a robustness check.
